run.answer_text:
Comparison: Payment Terms (Services Agreement) vs. Personal Data Breach Notice Duty (Data Processing Addendum)
Payment terms — Services Agreement [1]

The payment terms are concentrated in two clauses.

Clause 2 (Fees): "The Customer shall pay the Supplier a fee of GBP 4,500 per month, invoiced monthly in advance. Undisputed invoices must be paid within 45 days of the invoice date." (Source: [1])

Clause 3 (Late payment): "If an undisputed invoice is not paid when due, the Supplier may charge interest at 2% per month on the overdue amount until it is paid." (Source: [1])

Two further clauses touch payment indirectly:

Clause 5 (Termination / cure): "Either party may terminate this agreement immediately by written notice if the other party commits a material breach and fails to remedy it within 21 days of receiving notice of the breach." (Source: [1])

Clause 6 (Liability cap): "The Supplier's total liability under this agreement in any contract year is limited to the fees paid by the Customer in that year. Nothing in this agreement limits liability that cannot be limited by law." (Source: [1])

Task 1 flagged that the agreement contains no tax clause, no suspension right for non-payment, and no formal definitions of "Invoice Date," "Payment Date," or "Service Fees." The 45-day window in Clause 2 is measured from "the invoice date," a term the agreement does not separately define.

Personal data breach notice duty — Data Processing Addendum [2]

Only one clause in the addendum addresses breach notification.

Clause 4 (Personal data breach): "4. Personal data breach. The Processor shall notify the Controller without undue delay and in any event within 48 hours after becoming aware of a personal data breach." (Source: [2])

Task 2 noted that the clause is one-directional (Processor → Controller), sets no required content for the notice, imposes no cooperation or follow-up duty, and that the trigger term "personal data breach" is undefined within the addendum. Neither "personal data," "Processor," "Controller," nor "sub-processor" is defined in the document.

Side-by-side comparison
Dimension	Payment terms (Agreement [1])	Breach notice duty (DPA [2])
Obligated party	Customer pays Supplier (Clause 2)	Processor notifies Controller (Clause 4)
Trigger	Invoice issued (Clause 2); non-payment when due (Clause 3)	Processor becomes "aware of a personal data breach" (Clause 4)
Time limit	45 days from invoice date (Clause 2)	"without undue delay and in any event within 48 hours" of awareness (Clause 4)
Consequence of breach	2 % per-month interest (Clause 3); possible termination after 21-day cure (Clause 5)	No stated consequence or remedy in Clause 4
Liability / cap	Supplier liability capped at fees paid in the year (Clause 6)	No liability or cap provision in the addendum
Defined terms	"Invoice date" used but undefined; no "Payment Date" or "Service Fees" defined	"Personal data breach," "personal data," "Processor," "Controller" all used but undefined
Content / procedure	Amount fixed (GBP 4,500); invoicing in advance; no tax or suspension clause	No prescribed content, no cooperation duty, no follow-up obligation
Mutuality	Clause 5 cure/termination is mutual; payment and interest are one-directional	Breach notice is one-directional (Processor → Controller)
Key observations from the material

Timing granularity. The payment terms give a single fixed window (45 days from invoice date). The breach-notice duty uses a two-part standard — "without undue delay" plus a 48-hour outer limit — which is stricter and more nuanced. Task 1 noted that the payment window's reference point ("invoice date") is undefined; Task 2 noted that the breach trigger ("personal data breach") is likewise undefined. Both obligations therefore rest on an undefined reference point.

Consequences. Non-payment carries a defined financial penalty (2 % monthly interest) and a termination route (21-day cure). The breach-notice clause, by contrast, states no consequence for a late or absent notification and no cooperation or follow-up duty. This asymmetry is the most notable structural difference between the two provisions.

Liability interaction. Clause 6 caps the Supplier's total liability at the fees paid in any contract year. Because the DPA is a separate document and no result addressed whether the cap in Clause 6 extends to DPA obligations, it cannot be confirmed from these two documents alone whether a breach of Clause 4 would fall inside or outside that cap.

Gaps in both documents. Each document leaves its operative terms undefined: "invoice date" in the agreement, "personal data breach" in the addendum. Neither document addresses tax, suspension, notice content, or cooperation. A reader comparing the two for contract hygiene will find parallel drafting gaps.

What could not be established
Whether the liability cap in Clause 6 of the agreement governs DPA obligations, or whether the DPA contains its own cap, cannot be answered from these two documents.
The legal effect of the undefined terms ("invoice date," "personal data breach") in the parties' jurisdiction is not addressed by either sub-agent and would require further legal research.
No knowledge bases were available for this run, so no external authority on standard breach-notice or payment provisions was consulted.

Both tasks completed successfully and reported only what the two documents say; neither offered legal advice on application.

Employees get 25 working days of paid annual leave per leave year, plus 8 public holidays, and may carry over up to 5 days of unused leave into the next leave year (subject to a deadline and an ordering rule).

One thing to flag up front: the source is the file leave-policy.txt in the "Harness policies" knowledge base, and that file is itself labelled "FICTIONAL LEAVE POLICY (demonstration text only; no real company)" and concerns "Marmalade Mountain Foods Ltd." I report the figures exactly as written there; it is not confirmed to be a live policy. No documents were selected for this run, so the answer comes from that knowledge-base search only.

Annual leave entitlement

"Each full-time employee is entitled to 25 working days of paid annual leave in each leave year, plus 8 public holidays." (Source: [1])

Supporting terms from the same passage:

The leave year runs 1 April to 31 March: "The leave year runs from 1 April to 31 March" (Source: [1]).
Part-time employees get leave "in proportion to the days worked each week" (Source: [1]).
Mid-year joiners/leavers accrue "at the rate of 2.08 days for each completed month of service" (Source: [1]).
Carry-over

Employees may carry over up to 5 days, subject to a cap, a use-by deadline, and an ordering rule:

Cap and transfer: "An employee may carry over up to 5 days of unused annual leave into the next leave year." (Source: [1])
Deadline: "Carried-over days must be used by 30 June or they are lost." (Source: [1])
Ordering: "Carried-over days are taken before any new annual leave, so the oldest days are used first." (Source: [1])

A related condition on payment: "Annual leave is not paid out in place of time off, except that unused leave is paid when employment ends." (Source: [1])

What was not found

The sub-agent found no other carry-over figure or condition beyond the 5-day cap, the 30 June deadline, and the ordering rule. There is no separate "carryover" (one word) or "accrual" section; the 2.08-days-per-month figure applies only to mid-year joiners/leavers, not to carry-over. All points above are quoted from Source [1]; no general-knowledge content was used.

The sub-agent did not assess whether the policy is adequate or expand into other leave types.

## Payment terms — Services Agreement [1]

The payment terms are concentrated in two clauses.

- **Clause 6 (Liability cap):** "The Supplier's total liability under this agreement in any contract year is limited to the fees paid by the Customer in that year. Nothing in this agreement limits liability that cannot be limited by law." (Source: [1])

1. **Timing granularity.** The payment terms give a single fixed window (45 days from invoice date).
